faq.q: Does it search the internet or a database like Turnitin?
faq.a: No, and the tool is explicit about this. It only compares the text you paste in, or checks a single document for internal repetition. It cannot tell you whether your text matches a source you haven't provided, and it's not a substitute for institutional tools like Turnitin. Use it to compare drafts, spot accidental copying, and reduce repetition in your own writing.

faq.q: What similarity methods does it use?
faq.a: In Compare mode it runs four genuine algorithms and blends them into an overall score: Jaccard similarity (word-set overlap, 25%), cosine similarity on term frequencies (25%), longest common run of words (20%), and shared 3-gram and 5-gram overlap (30%). It lists the exact shared phrases, highlights matching sentences in green, and grades the result Original (<15%), Low (15–30%), Moderate (30–60%) or High (60%+).

faq.q: What does the Self-Check mode do?
faq.a: It scans one document for internal repetition: exact duplicate sentences, near-duplicate sentence pairs above a threshold you set (50–95%), and phrases (3-grams) that appear three or more times. It returns a repetition index with counts, lists the offending sentences and overused phrases, and shows readability stats. Useful for tightening an essay before submission.

faq.q: Can it detect paraphrasing, and is my text private?
faq.a: It detects word- and phrase-level overlap, so heavily paraphrased text with entirely different vocabulary may not be flagged — that needs semantic analysis it doesn't do. Everything runs in your browser; your text is never uploaded. Drafts are saved locally so you don't lose them, and you can copy or download a .txt report of the results.
